Distribution of Numerical Features¶

Plots histograms for the key numeric columns (age, bmi, bloodpressure, children, claim) to visualize how each variable is distributed across the dataset.

In [18]:
numeric_cols = ["age", "bmi", "bloodpressure", "children", "claim"]

df[numeric_cols].hist(bins=20, figsize=(12,8), color="skyblue", edgecolor="blue")
plt.suptitle("Distribution of Numerical Features", fontsize=16)
plt.show()

Distribution of Categorical Features¶

Plots count bar charts for the key categorical columns (gender, diabetic, smoker, region) to visualize how many records fall into each category.

In [19]:
cat_cols = ["gender", "diabetic", "smoker", "region"]

plt.figure(figsize=(12, 8))
for i, col in enumerate(cat_cols, 1):
    plt.subplot(2, 2, i)
    sns.countplot(data=df, x=col)
    plt.title(f"Distribution of {col}")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Smoker Rate and Average Claim by Region (Dual-Axis Chart)¶

Combines two metrics in one chart: bars show the smoker rate (%) per region on the left axis, while the red line shows the average claim ($) per region on the right axis — making it easy to compare both trends together.

In [41]:
fig, ax1 = plt.subplots(figsize=(8,5))

sns.barplot(data=region_stats, x="region", y="smoker_rate", ax=ax1, alpha=0.6)

ax2 = ax1.twinx()
sns.lineplot(data=region_stats, x="region", y="mean_claim", ax=ax2, color="red", marker="o")

ax1.set_ylabel("Smoker Rate (%)")
ax2.set_ylabel("Average Claim ($)")
plt.title("Smoker Rate and Average Claim by Region")
plt.show()

Import Machine Learning Libraries¶

Imports the tools needed to prepare data and build a prediction model:

  • train_test_split — splits data into training and testing sets
  • LabelEncoder — converts categorical text values (e.g., "yes"/"no") into numbers
  • StandardScaler — scales numeric features to a common range for better model performance
  • joblib — saves and loads the trained model for later use (e.g., in the prediction app)
In [43]:
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.preprocessing import LabelEncoder, StandardScaler
import joblib

Set Up Categorical Columns for Encoding¶

Lists the categorical feature columns (gender, diabetic, smoker) that need to be converted into numbers, and creates an empty dictionary to store each column's encoder for later use (e.g., in the prediction app).

In [49]:
cat_cols =["gender","diabetic","smoker"]
label_encoders={}

Encode Categorical Columns and Save Encoders¶

Converts each categorical column (gender, diabetic, smoker) into numeric values using Label Encoding, stores each fitted encoder for reference, and saves them to disk as .pkl files so the same encoding can be reused later by the prediction app.

In [50]:
for col in cat_cols:
    le = LabelEncoder()
    x[col] = le.fit_transform(x[col])
    label_encoders[col] = le
    joblib.dump(le, f"label_encoder_{col}.pkl")

Split Data into Training and Testing Sets¶

Splits the features (x) and target (y) into training and testing sets, reserving 20% of the data for testing the model's performance and 80% for training it.

In [53]:
x_train, x_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(x, y, test_size=0.2)

Set Up Numeric Columns for Scaling¶

Lists the numeric feature columns (age, bmi, bloodpressure, children) that need to be scaled, and initializes a StandardScaler to standardize them to a common range for better model performance.

In [54]:
num_cols = ["age","bmi","bloodpressure","children"]
scaler = StandardScaler()

Scale Numeric Features¶

Fits the scaler on the training data and applies it to standardize the numeric columns, then applies the same scaling to the test data (without re-fitting) to keep the transformation consistent between both sets.

In [55]:
x_train[num_cols] = scaler.fit_transform(x_train[num_cols])
x_test[num_cols] = scaler.transform(x_test[num_cols])

Save the Scaler¶

Saves the fitted scaler to disk as a .pkl file so the same scaling can be reused later (e.g., in the prediction app) without needing to refit it.

In [56]:
joblib.dump(scaler, "scaler.pkl")
Out[56]:
['scaler.pkl']

Import Model Building and Evaluation Libraries¶

Imports the tools needed to build, tune, and evaluate multiple prediction models:

  • numpy — numerical operations
  • LinearRegression — a simple baseline regression model
  • PolynomialFeatures — creates polynomial combinations of features for non-linear relationships
  • RandomForestRegressor — an ensemble tree-based model
  • SVR — Support Vector Regression model
  • GridSearchCV, cross_val_score — tools for tuning and validating model performance
  • mean_absolute_error, mean_squared_error, r2_score — metrics to evaluate prediction accuracy
  • XGBRegressor — a high-performance gradient boosting model
In [60]:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor
from sklearn.svm import SVR
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV, cross_val_score
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, mean_squared_error, r2_score
from xgboost import XGBRegressor

Define Model Evaluation Function¶

Creates a reusable function that takes a trained model, generates predictions on the test set, and returns three key performance metrics: R² (how well the model explains the variance), MAE (average prediction error), and RMSE (error size, penalizing larger mistakes more).

In [61]:
def evaluate_model(model, x_train, y_train, x_test, y_test):
    y_pred = model.predict(x_test)
    r2 = r2_score(y_test, y_pred)
    mae = mean_absolute_error(y_test, y_pred)
    rmse = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_test, y_pred))
    return {"r2": r2, "mae": mae, "rmse": rmse}

Initialize Results Storage¶

Creates an empty dictionary to store the performance metrics of each model tested, for easy comparison later.

In [62]:
results ={}

Train and Evaluate Multiple Regression Models¶

Trains four different models to predict claim amounts and stores each one's performance metrics for comparison:

  • Linear Regression — baseline model assuming a straight-line relationship
  • Polynomial Regression — tests degree 2 and 3 to capture non-linear patterns, keeping the best-performing degree
  • Random Forest — ensemble of decision trees, tuned via grid search over tree count, depth, and split settings
  • SVR (Support Vector Regression) — tuned via grid search over kernel type, regularization (C), and margin (epsilon)
  • XGBoost — gradient boosting model, tuned via grid search over tree count, depth, learning rate, and subsampling

Each model is evaluated using R², MAE, and RMSE, and results are stored in the results dictionary for side-by-side comparison.

In [63]:
lr = LinearRegression()
lr.fit(x_train, y_train)
results["linear regression"] = evaluate_model(lr, x_train, y_train, x_test, y_test)
print("linear regression model trained")

# --- Polynomial Regression (degree search) ---
best_poly_model = None
best_poly_score = -np.inf

for degree in [2, 3]:
    poly = PolynomialFeatures(degree=degree)
    x_train_poly = poly.fit_transform(x_train)
    x_test_poly = poly.transform(x_test)
    poly_lr = LinearRegression()
    poly_lr.fit(x_train_poly, y_train)
    score = poly_lr.score(x_test_poly, y_test)
    if score > best_poly_score:
        best_poly_score = score
        best_poly_model = (degree, poly, poly_lr)

degree, poly, poly_lr = best_poly_model
results[f"polynomial regression (deg={degree})"] = evaluate_model(
    poly_lr, poly.fit_transform(x_train), y_train, poly.transform(x_test), y_test
)
print("polynomial regression model trained")

# --- Random Forest ---
rf = RandomForestRegressor()
rf_params = {
    "n_estimators": [100, 200],
    "max_depth": [None, 10, 20],
    "min_samples_split": [2, 5],
    "min_samples_leaf": [1, 2]
}
rf_grid = GridSearchCV(rf, rf_params, cv=3, scoring="r2", n_jobs=-1, verbose=0)
rf_grid.fit(x_train, y_train)
best_rf = rf_grid.best_estimator_
results["random forest"] = evaluate_model(best_rf, x_train, y_train, x_test, y_test)
print("random forest training completed, best parameters:", rf_grid.best_params_)

# --- SVR ---
svr_model = SVR()
svr_params = {
    "kernel": ["rbf", "poly", "linear"],
    "C": [1, 10, 50],
    "epsilon": [0.1, 0.2, 0.5],
    "degree": [2, 3]
}
svr_grid = GridSearchCV(svr_model, svr_params, cv=3, scoring="r2", n_jobs=-1, verbose=0)
svr_grid.fit(x_train, y_train)
best_svr = svr_grid.best_estimator_
results["svr"] = evaluate_model(best_svr, x_train, y_train, x_test, y_test)
print("svr training complete, best parameters:", svr_grid.best_params_)

# --- XGBoost ---
xgb_model = XGBRegressor(objective="reg:squarederror")
xgb_params = {
    "n_estimators": [100, 200],
    "max_depth": [3, 5, 7],
    "learning_rate": [0.01, 0.05, 0.1],
    "subsample": [0.8, 1.0]
}
xgb_grid = GridSearchCV(xgb_model, xgb_params, cv=3, scoring="r2", n_jobs=-1, verbose=0)
xgb_grid.fit(x_train, y_train)
best_xgb = xgb_grid.best_estimator_
results["xgboost"] = evaluate_model(best_xgb, x_train, y_train, x_test, y_test)
print("xgboost training completed, best parameters:", xgb_grid.best_params_)

Compare Models in a Ranked Table¶

Converts the results dictionary into a DataFrame and sorts it by R² score (highest first), making it easy to see at a glance which model predicts claim amounts most accurately.

results_df = pd.DataFrame(results).T.sort_values(by="r2", ascending=False)

Store All Trained Models¶

Creates a dictionary mapping each model's name to its trained object, making it easy to reference, compare, or select any model by name later (e.g., when saving the best-performing one).

In [66]:
models = {
    "linear regression": lr,
    "polynomial regression": poly_lr,
    "random forest": best_rf,
    "svr": best_svr,
    "xgboost": best_xgb
}

Find the Best R² Score¶

Retrieves the highest R² score from the results table, identifying the top-performing model's accuracy.

Identify the Best-Performing Model¶

Filters the results table to find the row matching the highest R² score, identifying which model performed best.

top_model = results_df[results_df["r2"] == best_r2]

Select the Best-Performing Model Object¶

Retrieves the actual trained model object corresponding to the top row in the ranked results table (the model with the highest R² score), ready to be saved for use in the prediction app.

In [71]:
best_model = models[results_df.index[0]]
best_model

Save the Best Model to Disk¶

Saves the top-performing model to a .pkl file so it can be loaded later by the prediction app without needing to retrain, and prints a confirmation of which model was selected.

In [72]:
top_model_name = results_df.index[0]

joblib.dump(best_model, "best_model.pkl")
print(f"best model selected: {top_model_name}")
